hints: Think about what is kept constant in each snapshot. One graph freezes time and looks along the wave, the other watches one point as time passes.
Recall which quantity is a length along the wave and which is a time for one oscillation, so you can match $\lambda$ to distance and $T$ to time.
Remember both vertical axes measure the same thing - how far a particle is from equilibrium - and amplitude is the maximum value of this.
walkthrough:
**Picture the two different views**
Think of a progressive wave as a moving snake. You can either take a photograph at one instant and see its shape in space, or you can stare at one single point and watch it move up and down in time. Both views give a sine curve but the horizontal axis is different.

**Label the distance graph for wavelength**
For the displacement-distance graph: $$\text{y-axis = displacement, x-axis = distance}$$ Wavelength $\lambda$ is a length, so it belongs here. Mark it as the horizontal distance from one crest to the next crest, or one trough to the next. Amplitude $A$ is the vertical distance from the equilibrium line (0) to the top of a crest.

**Label the time graph for period**
For the displacement-time graph: $$\text{y-axis = displacement, x-axis = time}$$ Period $T$ is a time, so it belongs here. Mark it as the horizontal time from one crest to the next crest for that one particle. Amplitude $A$ is marked exactly the same way, from equilibrium to peak.

Final answer: Left graph: y-axis displacement, x-axis distance, $\lambda$ = distance between two adjacent peaks, $A$ = peak height from equilibrium. Right graph: y-axis displacement, x-axis time, $T$ = time between two adjacent peaks, $A$ = peak height from equilibrium.

hints: Start by following the wave made by the vibrator - what happens when it reaches the fixed clamp at X or Y?
Think about what happens when two identical waves travel in opposite directions through each other on the same string.
walkthrough:
**Reflection at the fixed ends**
The vibrator sends a progressive wave along the string. When it hits the fixed points X and Y it cannot pass through, so it reflects back. You now have two waves on the same string travelling in opposite directions with the same speed, frequency and wavelength.

**Superposition creates the stationary pattern**
Where the two oppositely travelling waves meet they superpose, meaning their displacements add. In most places they interfere constructively and destructively in a fixed pattern, giving fixed nodes of zero amplitude at X and Y and elsewhere, and antinodes of maximum amplitude in between. Because the pattern does not travel, it is a stationary wave.
Final answer: Progressive wave travels along string and reflects at fixed ends X and Y. Incident and reflected waves of same frequency superpose / interfere to form a stationary wave.

hints: Compare the elapsed time of 100 ms with the time for one full oscillation of 40 ms to find how many cycles have passed.
Visualise a particle starting at equilibrium - after a whole number of cycles it returns to the same state, so focus on what the extra half cycle does to displacement.
For total path length, count how many amplitudes are covered in one full back-and-forth cycle, then scale up to 2.5 cycles.
walkthrough:
**Find how many periods fit in 100 ms**
Each particle performs SHM with period $T = 40\text{ ms}$. Number of oscillations: $$N = \frac{100\text{ ms}}{40\text{ ms}} = 2.5$$ So the particle completes two full cycles plus one half cycle.

**Displacement after 2.5 cycles**
Displacement is position from equilibrium. Starting at 0, after any whole number of cycles you are back at 0. The extra 0.5 cycle takes you from 0 to max and back to 0 on the opposite side. So: $$\text{displacement at } t+100\text{ ms} = 0\text{ mm}$$ Do not confuse this with distance travelled.

**Total distance travelled**
Distance adds up all the path. In one period the particle goes 0 to +A to 0 to -A to 0, which is $4A$. $$\text{distance per period} = 4 \times 13 = 52\text{ mm}$$ $$\text{total distance} = 2.5 \times 52 = 130\text{ mm}$$
Final answer: 1. displacement = $0\text{ mm}$. 2. distance = $130\text{ mm}$.

hints: Use the given period of 40 ms to get frequency - remember to convert ms to s first.
Link the progressive wave speed of 30 m s-1 to frequency and wavelength with the wave equation.
Calculate the progressive wavelength from $v$ and $f$ before thinking about the stationary pattern.
Look at Fig. 4.2 and count how many wavelengths fit between the fixed ends X and Y.
walkthrough:
**Frequency from period**
Frequency is oscillations per second: $$f = \frac{1}{T}$$ $$T = 40\text{ ms} = 40 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}$$ $$f = \frac{1}{40 \times 10^{-3}} = 25\text{ Hz}$$

**Wavelength of the progressive wave**
Use the wave equation for the travelling waves that make the pattern: $$v = f\lambda$$ Rearranged: $$\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = \frac{30}{25} = 1.2\text{ m}$$ You can also think of it as $\lambda = vT = 30 \times 40 \times 10^{-3} = 1.2\text{ m}$.

**Read the stationary pattern length**
Fig. 4.2 shows nodes at X and Y with three half-loops in between. That is 1.5 full wavelengths: $$XY = 1.5\lambda$$ A common slip is to call XY one wavelength. Count nodes: X to first middle node is $\lambda/2$, and so on, giving $3 \times \lambda/2$.
Final answer: 1. frequency = $25\text{ Hz}$. 2. distance XY = $1.8\text{ m}$.
